His guidance to women is to put aside their dignity — along with anything else the situation may require.

Abby has good reason to doubt him, both as a professional and as a woman, but the ratings period proves her mistaken. Mike may be offensive, yet Sacramento viewers respond enthusiastically to him.

A sharper film might have found real comic energy in this setup: a refined female executive forced to manage a crude, reactionary male performer. Instead, despite being credited to three women writers, the movie goes out of its way to validate Mike’s stale sexist philosophy, while also failing to generate many laughs.

**Movie Review: “The Ugly Truth” pairs Katherine Heigl and Gerard Butler in a battle-of-the-sexes rom-com**

Released in 2009, **“The Ugly Truth”** is a glossy romantic comedy built around a familiar formula: a successful, tightly wound woman meets a crass, confident man who claims to understand what women really need to do to win men over. Sparks fly, insults land, lessons are learned — and, unsurprisingly, romance follows.

Katherine Heigl stars as **Abby Richter**, a television producer whose professional life is far more organized than her romantic one. She is smart, ambitious and deeply committed to finding the “perfect” man, though her checklist approach to dating has not exactly delivered results. Enter **Mike Chadway**, played by Gerard Butler, a blunt cable-access personality whose show, *The Ugly Truth*, reduces relationships to cynical rules about attraction, sex and gender roles.

When Mike is brought onto Abby’s morning show to boost ratings, she is horrified by his crude worldview. But after she develops a crush on her seemingly ideal neighbor, Colin, Mike offers to coach her in the art of seduction. Their arrangement becomes the movie’s central comic engine: Abby tries to follow Mike’s advice while resisting his philosophy, and Mike gradually reveals a softer side beneath the macho bravado.

Heigl is playing firmly within the persona that made her a rom-com staple in the late 2000s: polished, exasperated, career-driven and romantically unlucky. She brings energy and comic timing to Abby, especially in scenes where the character’s control begins to unravel. Still, the script often limits her to familiar beats — the perfectionist heroine who must loosen up, learn to be spontaneous and accept that love cannot be planned.

Butler’s Mike is the more polarizing figure. His character is written to be outrageous, sexist and deliberately provocative, and Butler leans into the swagger. He has enough charm to make some of Mike’s rough edges watchable, but the film frequently asks the audience to forgive behavior that feels less like playful bluntness and more like outdated gender commentary. His chemistry with Heigl gives the movie momentum, but Mike’s transformation from shock-jock cynic to romantic lead is not always convincing.

As a comedy, **“The Ugly Truth”** has a few effective moments, particularly when it embraces physical humor and the awkwardness of romantic performance. But its central ideas about men, women and dating feel broad even by romantic-comedy standards. The movie wants to satirize gender stereotypes while also relying heavily on them, and that tension weakens its impact.

Ultimately, **“The Ugly Truth”** is a slick but uneven entry in the battle-of-the-sexes genre. Heigl and Butler are committed performers with strong screen presence, and their back-and-forth gives the film its appeal. But beneath the glossy packaging and occasional laughs, the movie’s view of romance is more conventional — and more dated — than it seems to realize.

**Review: “The Ugly Truth” Is Exactly as Subtle as Its Title Suggests**

There are romantic comedies that sparkle, romantic comedies that coast on charm, and then there is **“The Ugly Truth,”** a film that seems to believe romance is best expressed through shouting, humiliation, and jokes that feel like they were discovered in a gym locker circa 1997.

Katherine Heigl stars as Abby Richter, a tightly wound morning-show producer whose checklist approach to love has yielded professional success and personal frustration. Enter Mike Chadway, played by Gerard Butler, a crass cable-access relationship guru whose entire philosophy can be summarized as: men are cavemen, women are delusional, and subtlety is for cowards. When Abby’s struggling TV show brings Mike aboard to boost ratings, the two clash, bicker, scheme, and — because this is a romantic comedy with a stopwatch — inevitably begin circling each other romantically.

The plot hinges on Mike coaching Abby to win over her handsome doctor neighbor, Colin, while also clearly becoming the person she is actually meant to fall for. This would be easier to buy if Mike weren’t introduced as less a charming rogue than a walking HR complaint with hair gel. His “truths” about dating are presented as brutally honest, but they mostly sound like advice shouted from a bachelor party bus stuck in traffic.

Heigl, who has proven she can be funny when given material with a pulse, spends much of the movie widening her eyes, clutching her dignity, and reacting as though every line of dialogue has just been dropped on her from a great height. Butler, meanwhile, attacks the role with the confidence of a man who has mistaken volume for charisma. Watching the two trade insults is less like witnessing crackling romantic tension and more like being seated between two people arguing over the last airport outlet.

The film’s centerpiece scenes aim for outrageous comedy, including the infamous vibrating-underwear dinner sequence, which is staged with all the sophistication of a whoopee cushion in formalwear. The movie clearly wants to be naughty and adult, but too often its R-rated edge feels like a teenager bragging because it learned a new word.

To be fair, “The Ugly Truth” moves quickly, and at **96 minutes**, it doesn’t overstay its welcome by much. It is rated **R for sexual content and language**, which is accurate, though perhaps it should also carry a warning for exposure to aggressively recycled gender stereotypes.

The biggest problem is that the film mistakes cynicism for wit and hostility for chemistry. Romantic comedies need friction, yes, but they also need a reason to root for the couple beyond the fact that the screenplay has locked them in the same room. By the time Abby and Mike arrive at their inevitable happy ending, the real ugly truth is that the audience has done most of the emotional labor for them.

counterfactuals.output:
**Review: “The Ugly Truth” is ugly, all right**

If romantic comedies are supposed to make you believe in love, *The Ugly Truth* seems more interested in making you believe in HR violations.

Starring Katherine Heigl as Abby, a tightly wound TV producer, and Gerard Butler as Mike, a proudly boorish “relationship expert” whose worldview appears to have been assembled from locker-room graffiti and rejected beer commercials, the film aims for a battle-of-the-sexes screwball romp. What it delivers instead is a parade of sexist punchlines, crude gags and romantic logic so strained it should come with a neck brace.

The premise is simple: Abby is unlucky in love because she has standards, plans and a personality. Mike, meanwhile, understands “the ugly truth” about men and women, which mostly boils down to “men are animals, women are manipulative, and everyone should stop pretending otherwise.” Naturally, the movie expects us to find him irresistible because he says offensive things loudly and Butler has enough charisma to keep the whole enterprise from collapsing immediately.

Heigl, who has often been better than the material handed to her, spends much of the film doing variations on flustered indignation while the script repeatedly punishes her character for being competent. Abby isn’t just professionally successful; she’s framed as romantically defective because she likes order and would prefer not to date a caveman in a V-neck. The movie calls this comedy. Others may call it a workplace lawsuit with a soundtrack.

The humor is aggressively crude, but not especially clever. There are vibrating underwear jokes, sexual misunderstandings, body-part quips and enough “men are simple, women are crazy” observations to fill a bargain-bin self-help book. Raunch can absolutely work in a romantic comedy when it reveals character or sharpens the satire. Here, it mostly lands with the elegance of a dropped dumbbell.

What’s most frustrating is that *The Ugly Truth* seems to think it’s reviving screwball comedy: fast-talking opposites, professional rivalry, romantic sparring, eventual surrender to chemistry. But classic screwball comedies had wit, rhythm and a sense that both leads were evenly matched. This film has shouting, smirking and a screenplay that mistakes hostility for sexual tension. Abby and Mike don’t banter so much as exchange insults until the plot decides they’re in love.

Butler does what he can with Mike, leaning into the character’s swagger and occasional glimpses of vulnerability. Heigl has solid comic timing, particularly when the movie lets her be exasperated rather than humiliated. Together, they generate some sparks, but the film keeps dousing them with another bucket of retrograde gender nonsense.

By the time *The Ugly Truth* lurches toward its inevitable romantic resolution, it hasn’t so much earned the pairing as worn down the audience’s resistance. The movie wants to say that men and women should accept each other’s flaws. What it actually suggests is that if a man is obnoxious long enough, he may eventually be rewarded with the woman he’s been condescending to for 90 minutes.

The ugly truth? This is a romantic comedy with too little romance, too little comedy and far too much confidence in jokes that should have stayed in 2009 — or better yet, never left the writers’ room.

**Movie Review: “The Ugly Truth” — A Rom-Com With Too Little Romance and Even Less Comedy**

Robert Luketic’s *The Ugly Truth* arrives dressed as a battle-of-the-sexes romantic comedy, but beneath its glossy studio sheen is a surprisingly sour, mechanical film that mistakes humiliation for humor and cynicism for insight. It wants to stand in the lineage of classics like *When Harry Met Sally…*, where sharp dialogue and emotional intelligence turned romantic incompatibility into something funny, tender and enduring. Instead, *The Ugly Truth* offers a string of vulgar set pieces and predictable reversals, hoping that volume and embarrassment will substitute for wit.

Katherine Heigl plays Abby Richter, a tightly wound television producer whose carefully managed life is disrupted by Mike Chadway, a crass cable-access personality played by Gerard Butler. Mike’s philosophy is blunt: men are simple, women are deluded, and romance is essentially a marketing problem. The film sets them up as ideological opposites, but the debate is rigged from the start. Abby is made shrill and socially inept so Mike’s boorish “truths” can seem effective, while Mike’s offensiveness is softened only because the plot insists he must eventually be lovable.

The problem is not that the film is raunchy. Romantic comedies can be frank, adult and even rude. *When Harry Met Sally…* famously built one of cinema’s great comic moments around a public fake orgasm in a deli. But that scene worked because it was rooted in character, timing and social observation. In *The Ugly Truth*, similar provocations feel less like comedy than punishment.

The film’s most notorious sequence involves Abby wearing remote-controlled vibrating underwear to a business dinner, only for a child to get hold of the controls. The scene escalates into a public display of mortification, with Abby writhing helplessly in front of colleagues and clients. It is staged as a comic centerpiece, but it has the desperate, airless quality of a sketch that cannot end quickly enough. Another embarrassing stretch has Abby remade under Mike’s tutelage — tighter dress, hair extensions, practiced laughter, strategic manipulation — as though the film’s idea of female empowerment is simply learning to perform male fantasy more efficiently.

There are other labored indignities: Mike’s on-air provocations, the awkward seduction coaching, the contrived romantic rival, and the climactic hot-air balloon sequence that tries to lift the story into old-fashioned romantic spectacle after spending most of its running time sneering at sentiment. By then, the film has not earned sincerity. It has merely run out of insults.

Heigl and Butler are not without screen presence. Heigl can play comic exasperation well, and Butler has a rakish energy that might have worked in a smarter, more balanced script. But their chemistry is repeatedly undercut by the screenplay’s insistence on reducing men and women to crude behavioral stereotypes. Where *When Harry Met Sally…* explored whether friendship, attraction and love could coexist, *The Ugly Truth* mostly asks whether a woman can be badgered into admitting that the obnoxious man was right all along.

Classic romantic comedies thrive on tension, but they also require generosity. They must like their characters enough to let them be foolish without making them contemptible. *The Ugly Truth* rarely manages that. It is slickly produced, briskly paced and intermittently energetic, but its worldview is too mean, its jokes too labored and its romance too unconvincing.

In the end, the ugly truth about *The Ugly Truth* is that it confuses abrasiveness with honesty. Compared with the elegance, warmth and verbal sparkle of the genre’s best examples, Luketic’s film feels less like a romantic comedy than a hostile negotiation with a kiss tacked on at the end.

counterfactuals.output:
“The Ugly Truth” wants to be a sparring-match romantic comedy, the kind where two opposites trade insults until the movie decides that hostility is just foreplay. Its central couple, Abby Richter (Katherine Heigl) and Mike Chadway (Gerard Butler), are built from familiar rom-com extremes: she’s a tightly wound TV producer who believes in checklists, compatibility and civilized courtship; he’s a proudly crude cable-access relationship guru who insists men are simple, sex-driven creatures and women would be happier if they stopped pretending otherwise.

Their relationship begins as workplace warfare. Abby is appalled when Mike is brought onto her struggling morning show to boost ratings with his macho “truths” about dating. Mike, in turn, treats Abby as a case study in female overthinking. When Abby develops a crush on her doctor neighbor, Mike coaches her through a makeover-and-manipulation campaign designed to help her “get” the guy. Naturally, the more Abby follows Mike’s advice, the more the film nudges her toward realizing that the man she actually has chemistry with is the one she supposedly can’t stand.

The problem is that the movie’s gender politics are both the joke and the trap. “The Ugly Truth” leans heavily on the idea that men and women are locked in a cynical marketplace: men want bodies, women want commitment, and romance is mostly a strategy game. Mike’s blunt sexism is often framed as outrageous but accurate, while Abby’s desire for emotional connection is mocked as naïve or controlling. The film occasionally tries to soften Mike by revealing insecurity beneath the swagger, and it gives Abby moments of professional competence and comic frustration. But too often, its laughs depend on reducing both sexes to caricatures.

Heigl and Butler do have energy together, and the movie is slickly paced, with a few broad comic set pieces aimed squarely at multiplex audiences. Still, the central romance asks viewers to accept verbal combat as intimacy and humiliation as flirtation. For a film about truth, it rarely feels honest about relationships; it feels more like a battle-of-the-sexes routine updated with raunchier dialogue.

“The Ugly Truth” is at its best when it lets Abby and Mike behave like flawed adults sparring through mutual attraction. It is at its weakest when it mistakes cynicism for insight.
